description: AEGIS: health monitoring for astronauts. A quick crew self-check plus a machine-learning early warning for solar radiation storms, built on NASA DONKI data. Team of two from IE University (web app + ML).
summary: Astronauts on long missions face five hazards named by NASA's Human Research Program: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. Today most problems are caught after the damage starts. e^x is a self-assessment app that warns before it: a clickable 3D body shows each astronaut's status against their own personal baseline, not generic ranges, with a plain-language explanation and a recommended action for every flag. A machine-learning early warning, trained on 15 years of NASA DONKI space-weather data, forecasts solar radiation storms; tested on 2024–2026 data it never saw, it warned on 16 of 17 storms, including the May 2024 superstorm, flagged about 39 hours before it arrived. A habitat watch shows how crew symptoms could be linked to environmental causes such as rising cabin CO₂ (simulated in our demo). Built for Moon and Mars missions, the same approach applies on Earth to hospital-at-home and remote crews.
details:
e^x is designed to ingest data from hardware already flying: the CSA Bio-Monitor smart shirt (heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, skin temperature), the Actiwatch (sleep), the Crew Active Dosimeter and Orion’s HERA (radiation), and the ISS cabin gas analyzers (CO₂). Today these sit in separate systems, and vitals are recorded mainly during exercise and spacewalks. e^x combines them with a 60-second daily check-in and flags drift from each astronaut’s personal baseline. Individual astronaut records are protected, so the demo crew is synthetic data shaped like these devices’ outputs. The radiation forecaster is trained and tested on real NASA DONKI space-weather data.

WHAT IT DOES

e^x helps astronauts assess their own health during a mission and tells them when a result needs attention from the crew or from flight surgeons.

• Crew overview: mission header and crew cards colored by each astronaut's worst status.

• 3D body map: click the brain (sleep, mood), heart (heart rate, blood pressure), blood (glucose), bones and muscle (exercise, estimated bone loss) or whole body (temperature, radiation dose). Each panel shows a status color, a chart over time, a simple explanation and a recommended action, with "notify flight surgeon" when red.

• Daily check-in with streaks and XP, so measuring becomes part of the routine; statuses re-score instantly.

• Personal-baseline alerts: a flag is raised when a metric drifts from that astronaut's own normal (robust rolling statistics), each with a severity and an action.

• Radiation module: cumulative dose against NASA's career limit, plus a forecast of the probability of a solar radiation storm after each flare, with watch and warning alert levels.

• May 2024 replay: a timeline of the May 2024 superstorm, held out from training. Flares appear, the probability rises, the shelter alarm fires, and the 10 May storm arrives about 39 hours after the first warning.

• Habitat watch: the habitat is treated as a fourth crew member. An anomaly detector (forecast residuals scored with a robust z-score), tuned and tested on NASA's labeled SMAP/MSL spacecraft telemetry, monitors simulated life-support data and shows how a crew symptom can be linked to a likely cause. In our demo, a crew member's sleep drop and a cabin CO₂ fault were planted separately and aligned on purpose to show how the link surfaces; it never changes a crew status or alert.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Python (pandas, scikit-learn) for data and ML; a React web app with a 3D body; JSON data contracts between the two so backend and frontend were built in parallel. Storm model: climatology baseline, logistic regression and gradient boosting compared on validation; the simpler logistic regression was kept because the booster's gain was inside our pre-set acceptance margin. Time-based split: trained to 2021, tuned on 2022–23, tested once on 2024–2026.

HELD-OUT RESULTS (2024–2026, never used for training or tuning; counted per storm)

The warning level caught 16 of 17 solar radiation storms with about 1 false alarm per month; the watch level caught 17 of 17 at about 6 per month. Brier skill vs climatology: 0.413. On the May 2024 superstorm, the 10 May storm was first warned about 39 hours ahead and the 13 May storm about 4.5 hours ahead; one X2.9 flare on 15 May triggered a warning with no storm. Honest limit: most of the skill comes from CME information; with flare size and position alone, skill drops to 0.055, so in operations e^x would rely on real-time CME detections.

HONEST DATA

Space-weather data is real (NASA DONKI, 2010–2026). Real astronaut health records are protected, so the crew is synthetic: values sit within normal healthy-adult ranges, with day-to-day persistence and physiologically motivated links between metrics (sleep, mood, heart rate, blood pressure), checked with a fidelity report. Habitat telemetry is simulated with planted faults; the detector's thresholds and metrics come from real NASA spacecraft telemetry. e^x is designed to ingest outputs of hardware already flying (Bio-Monitor shirt, Actiwatch, Crew Active Dosimeter, cabin gas analyzers), but has no live connection to ISS systems. Not medical advice.

IMPACT

For Artemis and Mars crews: earlier action on radiation, cardiovascular, sleep and environmental risks, with less dependence on a delayed link to Earth. On Earth: hospital-at-home programmes and remote crews (offshore, polar, military).
